concept.name: Upthrust after distribution
concept.definition: The Wyckoff event (UTAD) occurring in the latter stages of a distribution trading range, in which price breaks above range resistance and then fails, providing a definitive test of new demand before markdown. It is the distributional counterpart of the spring and terminal shakeout in accumulation.
concept.intuition: One last fake breakout at the top of a topping range, engineered to squeeze shorts and unload remaining stock onto breakout buyers before the decline.
concept.mechanics: Late in distribution (Phase C), price breaks above the range high, then reverses back into the range. The UTAD tests whether sufficient demand remains to support higher prices; its failure confirms supply dominance and often precedes the sign of weakness and markdown. Like springs, a UTAD is not a required element of distribution.
concept.failure_modes: A UTAD that holds above the range and is followed by strength invalidates the distribution reading; because it looks identical to a genuine breakout at first, shorting it early carries real squeeze risk.
concept.misconceptions: Distribution does not require a UTAD — the canonical schematics include distribution ranges with and without one — and a UTAD is not necessarily the range's absolute high.
concept.example: After five months of distribution between 136 and 150, a stock breaks to 155 for two days, then collapses back to 145 on heavy volume; the failed breakout is labeled a UTAD before the markdown begins.

citations.source: The Wyckoff Method: A Tutorial (StockCharts.com ChartSchool, by Roman Bogomazov and Michael Lipsett)
